scenes.tts: Press a Pa-sin-ee-an corpuscle and hold. The nerve fibre fires when the press starts, and again when it ends. It does not fire during the hold. A Pa-sin-ee-an corpuscle wraps one nerve ending in many concentric layers, like an onion. For decades, those layers got the credit. Was that right?

scenes.tts: The classic idea was a mechanical filter. In nineteen sixty-six, Low-en-stine and Skay-lak modelled the capsule. In their model, fluid between the layers supplies viscosity. The layers supply elasticity. A slow press is dissipated before it reaches the core. A fast tap gets through. For decades, this high-pass filter was the textbook explanation.

scenes.visual: Slow press fades out between the layers; fast tap reaches the terminal; a high-pass curve (in this sketch) closes the scene.

scenes.tts: A year earlier, in nineteen sixty-five, Low-en-stine and Mendel-son had removed most of the layers from isolated cat corpuscles. Then they held a press. After that, the generator potential, the graded depolarization of the nerve ending, decayed much more slowly. Later reviewers note this appeared mainly under intense compression. The ending typically still fired a single spike. So adaptation had two stages. One lay in the mechanics around the ending. The other lay in its spike-generating membrane.

scenes.tts: In twenty twenty-five, the test moved to duck bill skin. Ziolkowski and colleagues recorded directly from the nerve terminal inside Herbst corpuscles, the bird version of Pa-sin-ee-an ones. The skin came from late embryos, and the recordings were ex vivo. They removed the outer core and left the inner core's lamellar cells in place. The fast transduction current stayed. The frequency tuning did not change significantly.

scenes.tts: Slower inactivation appeared only as decapsulated terminals deteriorated. So a dying terminal can look like one that lost its filter. That is one reading of nineteen sixty-five. Keep the scope. This is a bird corpuscle, ex vivo. It does not show that the capsule does nothing in a cat or a human hand.

scenes.tts: So what are the lamellar cells for? These flattened cells wrap the nerve terminal. In duck bill skin, they respond to force too. Depolarizing one Grandry lamellar cell could make its afferent fire. But in duck, the delay ran from twenty milliseconds to about nine seconds. A two hundred hertz vibration repeats every five milliseconds. So lamellar cells may set the terminal's sensitivity, not carry each cycle. Keep this. In duck corpuscles, with the outer core gone, the terminal still adapts fast.
